title: 3-Read Friday #77: Checks for Understanding, Cognitive Load Theory, and Borrowed Thought
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #77 links three posts on the theme of what actually strengthens learning versus what merely feels productive. Mike Hobbiss extends his own earlier work on attention cueing to show that a well-designed check for understanding delivers three distinct benefits at once - assessment information for the teacher, retrieval practice for material already covered, and 'test expectancy' effects that improve attention and learning of material still to come. Paul Kirschner surveys John Sweller's 2023 retrospective on Cognitive Load Theory, showing how the theory has grown stronger precisely by absorbing its own replication failures and integrating insights from evolutionary psychology, arriving at the conclusion that effective teaching means aligning instruction with the actual architecture of human cognition rather than chasing trends. David Didau responds to the widely-discussed 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' study, arguing that using AI before doing one's own thinking produces a kind of 'cognitive debt' - fluent-seeming output without the underlying understanding - while using AI after independent effort appears to cause no such erosion. Barton's framing draws all three together around a single insight: genuine learning requires effortful engagement with material, whether that effort comes from anticipating a test, wrestling with cognitive load, or thinking before reaching for AI.
points: Mike Hobbiss identifies three distinct benefits of a well-timed check for understanding: it provides assessment-for-learning information, it functions as retrieval practice for prior content, and - the least obvious - it improves attention and learning of content that hasn't been presented yet, via 'test expectancy.'

Paul Kirschner's key takeaway from Sweller's 2023 retrospective: Cognitive Load Theory grew stronger specifically because it absorbed replication failures as signals pointing to missing variables, rather than treating them as threats to the theory's validity.

Kirschner highlights Sweller's integration of David Geary's evolutionary distinction between biologically primary knowledge (like spoken language, acquired naturally) and biologically secondary knowledge (like algebra, which must be explicitly taught) as a major theoretical expansion.

David Didau's central argument from the 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' study: using AI before independently attempting a task produces measurable 'cognitive debt' - lower neural coherence, weaker recall, less felt ownership - while using AI after first thinking independently showed no such erosion.

Didau's practical implication: schools should not ban AI outright but must teach students to think first and use AI to refine or extend that thinking afterward, since sequencing - not simply access - determines whether AI amplifies or hollows out learning.
quotes: Mike outlines three benefits from an easily implementable strategy: tell students they will be tested on the information you are about to present.
Paul provides a fascinating insight into the latest developments in Cognitive Load Theory and the implications for instruction.
This quote hit home for me: effective teaching is not about showmanship or trend-chasing, it is about aligning instruction with the reality of how our brains work.
I recently wrote about the perils of students cognitively outsourcing their homework to ChatGPT. David delves into this issue further.
I'm a sucker for reading about attention and checks for understanding, and this post by Mike ticks both boxes.
